chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Numerical Methods? Foundations of Option Pricing Beyond Closed-Form

lessons.title: Case Study: Pricing an American Put on a Nifty Stock Where Black-Scholes Fails

children.text: Three ideas from this chapter are about to come together. Lesson 1 argued that Black-Scholes cannot see the value of early exercise. Lesson 2 built the machinery, replicate the payoff, price under risk-neutral probability, that correctly prices one single step of time. Lesson 3 showed that repeating that machinery over many discrete steps is the general strategy behind every numerical method in this course. This lesson puts all three to work on one concrete case, computed entirely by hand, so the early-exercise premium stops being an abstract idea and becomes an actual rupee number.

Hind Metals Ltd is a hypothetical Nifty 50 metals-and-mining constituent, standing in here for the kind of commodity-linked, swing-prone stock this scenario needs. Its shares trade at ₹200. A trading desk holds an American put struck at ₹200, at the money today, with two steps of time left before expiry, each step wide enough for the stock to move roughly 15% in either direction, a realistic single-step swing for a metals name reacting to global commodity prices. Chapters 2 and 3 build the full, formal machinery for calibrating step size and move size from actual volatility. Here, to keep the arithmetic in view, the up and down moves are simply given.

cells: −13.04% (×0.8696, the reciprocal of the up move)

children.text: Because the down move is exactly the reciprocal of the up move, an up followed by a down lands back on the starting price, the lattice recombines instead of branching into four separate endpoints. That gives three distinct prices after two steps, not four.

body.caption: Prices and put payoffs after two steps

The risk-neutral probability for this lattice, using the same no-arbitrage logic as Lesson 2, extended to multiplicative up and down factors. Chapter 2 derives and calibrates u, d, and p formally; this is the direct calculation for this specific case.

children.text: Stepping Backward: Where the American Value Pulls Away

Backward induction starts from the known payoffs at expiry and works one step back at a time. At each node along the way, two numbers get compared: the hold value, the discounted expected value of continuing to hold the option, exactly as Lesson 2 computed it, and the intrinsic value, what the put is worth if exercised immediately. An American option takes whichever is larger. A European option cannot exercise early, so it only ever uses the hold value until expiry itself.

At the node reached after one up move, the stock sits at ₹230, above the ₹200 strike. The put's intrinsic value there is ₹0, and its hold value is also ₹0, since both paths forward from here end with a ₹0 payoff. Nothing interesting happens at this node, for either an American or a European holder.
The node reached after one down move is where the whole case study lives. The stock has fallen to ₹173.91.

stats.label: Hold value at this node
stats.context: Discounted expected value of the two payoffs one step ahead, ₹0 and ₹48.77, under risk-neutral probability

stats.label: American value at this node
stats.context: The higher of the two. Early exercise is optimal here

body.text: This is the exact mechanism from Lesson 1 showing up as a number. The stock has already fallen enough that the remaining downside, capped by zero, is worth less to a holder than simply cashing in ₹26.09 today and earning risk-free interest on it for the one step left. A European holder has no choice in the matter and is stuck with the ₹16.56 hold value. An American holder exercises and locks in ₹26.09, a difference of ₹9.53 at this one node alone.

children.text: One more discounting step, from the two nodes just computed back to today, finishes the tree. The American side carries forward ₹26.09 from the down node, since that early exercise already happened in the model's logic. The European side is forced to carry forward the smaller ₹16.56 hold value from that same node, because a European put cannot act on the early-exercise opportunity a step early.

stats.label: American put, today
stats.context: Discounts forward ₹0 (up node) and ₹26.09 (down node, exercised)

stats.label: European put, today
stats.context: Discounts forward ₹0 (up node) and ₹16.56 (down node, hold only). This is what the tree's European side, and by extension Black-Scholes, would price

stats.label: Early-exercise premium
stats.value: ₹3.23, about 58% more than the European price
stats.context: The value Black-Scholes cannot see, made concrete

body.text: Two steps is deliberately coarse, chosen to keep every number checkable by hand. A real desk would run this same logic over dozens or hundreds of steps, exactly what Chapter 2 builds toward and Chapter 3's convergence lesson formalizes. The premium's exact size would shift with more steps. The fact that a real, positive premium exists here, and comes entirely from a single node's early-exercise decision, would not.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why was early exercise optimal at the down node after one step, but irrelevant at the up node?
options: Because the risk-free rate is different at each node
Because the put is in the money only at the down node, where the hold value has fallen below the intrinsic value
Because American options can only be exercised after a down move by convention
Because the up node has a higher risk-neutral probability attached to it
body.explanation: At the up node the put is out of the money, intrinsic value is zero, so there is nothing to gain by exercising. At the down node the put is deep in the money, and the stock has fallen enough that the remaining time value from waiting is worth less than exercising now and earning interest on the proceeds. Early exercise only ever gets checked, and only ever matters, where the option is meaningfully in the money.

body.title: Is the Premium Just Noise?
body.scenario: A colleague looks at this two-step example and argues that since it is so coarse, only two steps for the entire life of the option, the ₹3.23 early-exercise premium is probably just an artifact of using too few steps rather than a real feature of the option.
body.prompt: How would you respond, and what would actually settle the question?
body.modelAnswer: The premium is not an artifact of coarseness, it comes from a genuine economic mechanism: a deep in-the-money put whose remaining downside is bounded by zero is worth more exercised than held, regardless of how finely time is sliced. What is fair to question is the precise size of ₹3.23, since that number depends on the coarse two-step setup. The way to settle it is exactly what Chapter 3 does, rebuild the same case with many more steps and check whether the premium stabilizes to a similar order of magnitude rather than vanishing. It will not vanish, because the mechanism generating it, comparing hold value against intrinsic value at every node, does not depend on how many steps are used.

body.text: An American put's extra value is not theoretical. It shows up as a real, computable number the moment a model is allowed to check for early exercise at every node instead of only at expiry, which is precisely what Black-Scholes never does.

points: Backward induction compares hold value against intrinsic value at every node. An American option takes the higher of the two; a European option is stuck with the hold value until expiry.
In this two-step case, early exercise became optimal at exactly one node, the one where the stock had fallen enough that the remaining time value dropped below the immediate exercise value.
That single node's decision was enough to push the American put's price to ₹8.86 against a European price of ₹5.62, a premium of ₹3.23, roughly 58% higher.

The exact rupee figure depends on the coarseness of this two-step example, but the existence of a positive early-exercise premium does not, it comes from a real economic mechanism, not from the number of steps used.

Chapters 2 and 3 formalize everything used informally here: calibrating realistic up and down moves from volatility, building trees with many more steps, and confirming that this same mechanism holds up as the model gets finer.
